design_detail: Compilation that the authors call a meta-analysis: published post-mortem drug concentrations in specimens other than blood and urine, found by keyword searching and reference lists (no database or dates named), combined with results from the authors' laboratory, the national post-mortem toxicology database of the Finnish National Institute for Health and Welfare (THL), 2000–2018. It covers the 50 compounds (49 drugs and the metabolite norbuprenorphine) most often quantified in non-blood specimens in that database; drugs of abuse without an available or reasonable normal range were excluded, so there is no cocaine, MDMA or cannabinoid, while amphetamine, methamphetamine, morphine, codeine, fentanyl, methadone, oxycodone, buprenorphine, tramadol and several benzodiazepines are included. Summaries: Table 2, each drug's median concentration in each specimen divided by the median femoral-blood concentration reported by Launiainen & Ojanperä (2014), unpaired; Table 3, the median of within-case specimen-to-femoral ratios where a literature source gave both values (paired, literature only); Tables 4–5, ratios or means adopted from sources that reported only aggregates. Across-drug summaries are means, number-weighted means, medians and, in Table 2, medians rescaled so that femoral blood equals 1. No weighting by study, intervals, heterogeneity statistics, risk-of-bias assessment or sensitivity analysis.
can_establish: Typical (median) concentrations in ten post-mortem specimens relative to femoral blood for 50 compounds, from a large compilation dominated by published case reports and series; and, from the paired within-case data (Table 3), that the ratio to femoral blood differs between drugs by tenfold or more for most specimens.
cannot_establish: How far a single case can deviate from a median ratio (no ranges, percentiles or intervals are given); whether ratios differ between poisoning and other deaths or with time since death (neither was classified); whether the literature compiled is complete or representative (no systematic search, no appraisal of sources); or anything about the drugs left out, including cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids.

sample.recruitment: Literature: studies and case reports giving post-mortem drug concentrations in specimens other than blood or urine, found with keywords such as post-mortem, concentration, tissue, matrix and specimen and by following references (PDF p. 4). Own data: THL's national post-mortem toxicology database, with toxicology in about 6,500 deaths a year, requested by the forensic pathologist performing the medico-legal investigation (PDF p. 4), and analyses in 118,990 cases in 2000–2018; for the 50 drugs, 1,442 results in non-blood specimens (PDF p. 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Drugs: the 50 with the most quantitative results in specimens other than post-mortem blood, urine or vitreous humour in the THL database; drugs of abuse for which a normal range is not available or reasonable were excluded (PDF p. 4). Sources: studies presenting only blood or urine concentrations were excluded (PDF p. 4). No criteria on cause of death, time since death, sampling site, analytical method, language or date; the reference list runs from 1964 (ref. 102, PDF p. 17) to 2018 and includes German-language case reports (e.g. refs 89–91 and 95, PDF p. 16).
sample.demographics: Not reported: the age, sex and cause of death of the compiled cases are not given.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The numbers of records screened and excluded are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Published cases are mostly fatal poisonings: in Table 2 the femoral-blood concentrations of the compiled cases had a median ratio of 3.35 (mean 10.55) to the reference medians, which were medians regardless of cause of death, and reached 95.0 for metoprolol and 111.5 for propranolol (PDF pp. 42–43); the authors acknowledge that the literature centres on intoxications (PDF pp. 7–8). The laboratory's own non-blood results come from a service that analyses other matrices when post-mortem blood is not available (PDF p. 5), which the Introduction associates with decomposed, burned or otherwise destroyed bodies (PDF p. 2). In Table 2 each specimen's median comes from a different set of cases, so the unpaired ratios mix differences in case selection with differences between specimens.

exposure.measurement: Concentrations as reported by each source; the analytical methods of the literature sources are not recorded. THL data: liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry with electrospray ionization; samples taken at autopsies performed on average 7 days after death and stored refrigerated until analysis (PDF p. 4). Whether morphine results are free or total (including conjugated) morphine is not stated.
exposure.polysubstance: Co-administration of other drugs is named as a source of variation but was mostly not reported by the sources and was not analysed (PDF pp. 6, 8).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (deaths). Time since death was often not given in the sources and can range from a few hours to months (PDF p. 8); THL autopsies took place on average 7 days after death (PDF p. 4).

comparison.controls: Femoral blood as the reference specimen: in Table 2, the median femoral-blood concentration regardless of cause of death from Launiainen & Ojanperä (2014), listed in Table 1; in Table 3, the femoral-blood concentration measured in the same case.
comparison.matching: Within-case pairing in Table 3 only (4,960 results from literature sources).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Cause of death, time since death, sampling site and procedure, co-ingested drugs, metabolism and genetic background, age, disease and the circumstances of death were unavailable for most cases (PDF p. 8).

outcomes.instruments: Ratio of the drug concentration in other blood (such as cardiac blood), vitreous humour, skeletal muscle, liver, kidney, brain, heart, lung, spleen and bile to that in femoral blood, by drug (Tables 2–5); across-drug summaries as mean, number-weighted ('adjusted') mean, median and, in Table 2, median rescaled so that femoral blood equals 1 ('adjusted median') (PDF pp. 43–44).
outcomes.validity_norms: Femoral blood is treated as the reference matrix. The Table 2 denominators are medians across all causes of death, while the numerators come mostly from poisoning case literature; rescaling to femoral blood equal to 1 assumes the same case-mix inflation for every specimen, which is not tested.
outcomes.operationalization: A specimen is judged more useful for quantitative interpretation the closer its median ratio is to that of femoral blood; the recommended order of specimens when femoral blood is unavailable is presented as following from this (PDF p. 7).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical tests). A correlation of the ratios with volume of distribution, half-life and log P was examined, but neither the method nor the data are shown (PDF p. 6).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; duplicate screening or data extraction is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Paired within-case medians across drugs (Table 3, PDF p. 44), with the number of results: other blood 1.27 (576), vitreous humour 0.45 (356), muscle 0.99 (385), liver 5.06 (1,697), kidney 2.86 (401), brain 1.84 (565), heart 2.03 (185), lung 3.69 (187), spleen 4.25 (71), bile 5.52 (537); number-weighted means 1.52, 0.53, 1.09, 8.67, 3.99, 2.33, 4.52, 9.90, 10.35 and 66.99. Unpaired rescaled medians (Table 2, PDF p. 43): other blood 1.57, vitreous humour 0.30, muscle 0.54, liver 6.30, kidney 4.12, brain 2.21, heart 2.50, lung 4.86, spleen 2.66, bile 8.37. Between drugs (Table 3): liver from 0.95 (pregabalin, 3 results) to 54.29 (sertraline, 29); vitreous humour from 0.03 (sertraline, 11) to 1.59 (fentanyl, 6); other blood from 0.90 (hydroxyzine, 6) to 14.61 (chloroquine, 2). No ranges, percentiles or confidence intervals are given for any drug or specimen.
analysis.selective_reporting: The correlation with pharmacokinetic parameters is reported only as data not shown (PDF p. 6); no per-case or per-source values or spreads are given. The authors call the unpaired Table 2 their main result (PDF p. 6) rather than the paired Table 3.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Many drug–specimen cells rest on one to three results (for example, in Table 3, heart for morphine and spleen for fentanyl, one result each); the authors call such ratios only suggestive (PDF p. 8).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across drugs, the paired data put the median specimen-to-femoral ratio near 1 for muscle (0.99) and other blood (1.27), at about half for vitreous humour (0.45), near 2 for brain (1.84) and heart (2.03), and between 2.9 and 5.5 for kidney, lung, spleen, liver and bile, with tenfold or larger differences between drugs in most specimens; how far individual cases scatter around these medians is not reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract and Conclusions present a meta-analysis and group vitreous humour with the specimens whose concentrations are similar to femoral blood, slightly lower (PDF pp. 2, 8), although its typical concentration was about a half (paired) to a third (unpaired) of femoral blood. The recommended order (other blood, muscle, vitreous humour, brain, heart, spleen, kidney, liver, bile; PDF pp. 2, 7, 8) is said to follow from closeness to femoral blood, but in ratio terms brain and heart are closer than vitreous humour in both tables (editors' calculation: Table 3, brain 1.84-fold and heart 2.03-fold above against vitreous 2.2-fold below), and lung, also tabulated, is left out. The authors call the unpaired Table 2 the main result and the paired Table 3 very similar (PDF p. 6); across drugs the summaries are similar, but drug by drug they can differ more than tenfold (codeine, other blood: 16 times femoral blood in Table 2 against a paired median of 1.16 in Table 3; editors' calculation). The Introduction's aim of understanding the difference between normal and fatal concentrations in alternative specimens (PDF p. 3) could not be pursued, because cause of death could not be classified (PDF p. 8). The list of drugs with the highest ratios (PDF p. 7) partly reflects how far the literature cases' own femoral blood exceeded the reference medians.

timeline.event: Pounder & Jones, four-case series showing several-fold site differences in post-mortem blood; one of this compilation's doxepin sources (ref. 180).

Leikin & Watson's narrative review lists single approximate heart-to-peripheral blood ratios for about 100 drugs; for several drugs in both papers they are higher than this compilation's paired other-blood medians (for example oxycodone 3.1 against 1.19, methamphetamine 2.4 against 1.50).
Launiainen & Ojanperä, source of the femoral-blood medians regardless of cause of death that form the Table 2 denominators and Table 1 (not read by this reader).
Borra et al., a review of 50 years of post-mortem redistribution research (on the reading list; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: A widely usable lookup of typical specimen-to-femoral ratios for medicines, of which the paired Table 3 is the better-founded part. It gives no spread for any ratio, does not separate poisoning from other deaths and excludes cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids. The femoral-blood reference study it depends on (Launiainen & Ojanperä 2014) and the 2026 review (Borra et al.) are on the reading list.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the accepted manuscript.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the accepted manuscript; the version of record was not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors at the Forensic Toxicology Unit of the National Institute for Health and Welfare (THL), Helsinki (PDF p. 1), which keeps the national database included here. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective multi-centre post-mortem study taking femoral blood and each alternative specimen in the same consecutive deaths, recording cause of death, time since death and storage, analysed with one validated method, and reporting for each drug the full spread of within-case ratios (for example a 90% prediction interval) separately for poisonings and other deaths; and the same for cocaine, MDMA, cannabinoids and newer synthetic drugs, which this compilation excludes.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: By analogy: population (post-mortem cases of any cause), compounds (50 named), comparator (femoral blood) and outcome (concentration ratio) are stated (PDF pp. 3–4), though case-level criteria are not.
Single case reports, case series and the laboratory database are pooled without explanation.
Keywords and reference lists only; no database, dates, language policy or grey-literature search stated (PDF p. 4).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Only reference numbers per drug (Table 2); no design, number of cases, cause of death, time since death, sampling site or method for any source.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Medians of pooled individual results, unweighted by source; the main (Table 2) ratios are unpaired against an external all-cause reference; no variance, interval or heterogeneity measure.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Limitations are listed (PDF pp. 7–8), but the recommended order is drawn without regard to the quality or case mix of the sources.
Large variation is acknowledged and a correlation with pharmacokinetic parameters was looked for (data not shown); discrepancies between Tables 2, 3 and 4 for the same drug are not examined.
The over-representation of poisonings in the literature is noted (PDF pp. 7–8) but its effect on the ratios is not investigated.

domains.note: Neither statement appears in the accepted manuscript; the version of record was not read.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 is applied by analogy, because the paper presents itself as a meta-analysis of literature data (as with Strömmer 2020, senior decision 74); items written for reviews of interventions are read for a compilation of concentration ratios. All seven critical items are unmet, which gives critically low confidence. This is a judgment on how far the pooled ratios can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not on the paper's usefulness: it is a large, transparent table of typical values. Citable for: typical (median) ratios of drug concentrations in alternative post-mortem specimens to femoral blood, preferably the paired values of Table 3 with their numbers of results; the wide variation between drugs; the authors' recommended order of specimens, as their recommendation. Not citable for: the ratio to expect in an individual case, differences between fatal and non-fatal concentrations, drugs not included (cocaine, MDMA, cannabinoids), or the recommended order as an evidence-based ranking.

key_findings.finding: The compilation comprises 10,993 analytical results from 5,375 post-mortem cases in 388 studies, including results from the authors' laboratory database (2000–2018), for 50 commonly used drugs in femoral blood, other blood (such as cardiac blood), vitreous humour, muscle, liver, kidney, brain, heart, lung, spleen and bile.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; also Material and Methods, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Where a source gave the femoral-blood concentration of the same case (4,960 results, literature only), the median specimen-to-femoral ratios across drugs were: other blood 1.27, vitreous humour 0.45, muscle 0.99, liver 5.06, kidney 2.86, brain 1.84, heart 2.03, lung 3.69, spleen 4.25 and bile 5.52 (number of results 576, 356, 385, 1,697, 401, 565, 185, 187, 71 and 537).
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion, 6th paragraph (PDF p. 6); Table 3, rows Median and Adjusted mean (PDF p. 44)

key_findings.finding: Unpaired comparison: each specimen's median concentration divided by the reference median femoral-blood concentration (reference 7, Launiainen & Ojanperä), then rescaled so that femoral blood equals 1, gave other blood 1.57, vitreous humour 0.30, muscle 0.54, liver 6.30, kidney 4.12, brain 2.21, heart 2.50, lung 4.86, spleen 2.66 and bile 8.37. Before rescaling, femoral blood in the compiled cases had a median ratio of 3.35 (mean 10.55) to the reference medians.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows mean, median and adjusted median; Results and discussion, 5th paragraph (PDF p. 6)
key_findings.note: The text gives brain as 2.11 (PDF p. 6); the table's 2.21 matches 7.42 divided by 3.35 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Ratios vary widely between drugs (Table 3, number of results in brackets): liver from 0.95 (pregabalin, 3) and 1.25 (tramadol, 11) to 54.29 (sertraline, 29) and 41.00 (lidocaine, 41); vitreous humour from 0.03 (sertraline, 11) and 0.15 (amitriptyline, 20) to 1.59 (fentanyl, 6) and 1.44 (oxycodone, 8); muscle from 0.16 (codeine, 14) to 7.24 (clozapine, 1); other blood from 0.90 (hydroxyzine, 6) to 14.61 (chloroquine, 2); bile up to 616.67 (buprenorphine, 19) and 1094 (norbuprenorphine, 13).

Opioids, paired medians (Table 3, number of results in brackets): morphine other blood 1.26 (53), vitreous humour 0.40 (120), muscle 1.00 (135), liver 2.11 (339), kidney 4.39 (43), brain 0.51 (205), lung 1.60 (40), bile 38.69 (158); codeine other blood 1.16 (12), vitreous 1.00 (20), muscle 0.16 (14), liver 2.11 (61), bile 5.52 (46); fentanyl other blood 1.15 (33), vitreous 1.59 (6), liver 6.18 (120), heart 5.12 (14), bile 3.51 (20); methadone other blood 1.17 (13), muscle 0.73 (11), liver 5.00 (46), brain 1.82 (19), bile 5.94 (14); oxycodone other blood 1.19 (16), vitreous 1.44 (8), liver 1.66 (30), bile 5.64 (14); buprenorphine liver 11.42 (8), bile 616.67 (19).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows Morphine, Codeine, Fentanyl, Methadone, Oxycodone and Buprenorphine
key_findings.note: Whether morphine values are free or total morphine is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Amphetamines and benzodiazepines, paired medians (Table 3, number of results in brackets): amphetamine other blood 1.43 (6), vitreous humour 1.11 (3), muscle 0.75 (5), liver 3.50 (51), brain 1.70 (25); methamphetamine other blood 1.50 (9), vitreous 0.89 (4), muscle 1.09 (9), liver 3.48 (63), kidney 2.27 (17), brain 2.64 (34); diazepam other blood 0.95 (11), muscle 0.56 (9), liver 3.70 (22); alprazolam other blood 1.23 (2), vitreous 0.26 (2), liver 4.88 (15).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows Amphetamine, Methamphetamine, Diazepam and Alprazolam

key_findings.finding: Drugs of abuse for which a normal range is not available or reasonable were excluded; the 50 compounds (49 drugs and norbuprenorphine) include amphetamine, methamphetamine, opioids and benzodiazepines but no cocaine, MDMA or cannabinoid.
key_findings.locator: Material and Methods, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4); Table 1 (PDF p. 41)

key_findings.finding: The authors report no apparent correlation between the ratios and volume of distribution, half-life or log P in any specimen, and conclude that these parameters cannot predict tissue-to-femoral ratios; the data are not shown.

When femoral blood is unavailable, the authors recommend this order of specimens for quantitative analysis: other blood, muscle, vitreous humour, brain, heart, spleen, kidney, liver, bile. Liver remains suitable for screening but is not recommended for quantitation, bile ratios are high and hard to interpret, and in probable fatal intoxication all available specimens should be measured.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion, 9th and 10th paragraphs (PDF p. 7); Conclusions, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 8); also Abstract (PDF p. 2)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: cases could not be classified by cause of death because it was often not given; time since death was often not given and can range from hours to months; co-ingestion, metabolism and genetic background, age, disease and circumstances of death were mostly unreported; some drug–specimen cells have few results, making those ratios only suggestive; sampling site and procedure varied between cases.
key_findings.locator: Limitations (one paragraph, PDF p. 7, continuing on PDF p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Compounds with the highest mean ratios regardless of specimen, for which the authors advise caution in judging possible intoxication: buprenorphine, chloroquine, propranolol, orphenadrine, metoprolol, norbuprenorphine, clozapine, zopiclone, chlorpromazine, verapamil, hydroxyzine, oxazepam, temazepam, trimipramine and diltiazem.
key_findings.note: The metric is not defined and verapamil is listed twice. For several of these drugs the literature cases' own femoral blood was far above the reference median in Table 2 (propranolol 111.5, metoprolol 95.0, chloroquine 24.6; PDF p. 42 and 43), so the high ratios partly reflect case selection.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the rescaled median for brain as 2.11, while Table 2 gives 2.21.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table value is consistent with the brain median of 7.42 divided by the femoral median of 3.35 (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The caption of Table 3 says its data are also included in Table 2, but Table 3 has rows for ephedrine and moclobemide, which appear in neither Table 1 nor Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: The tables were not assembled from one consistent dataset; the across-drug summaries of Tables 2 and 3 cover slightly different sets of compounds.

reporting_issues.issue: The text calls the paired ratios of Table 3 very similar to those of Table 2 (PDF p. 6), but for single drugs the unpaired Table 2 implies very different ratios: codeine other blood 6.4 and femoral blood 0.4 in Table 2, but a paired median of 1.16 in Table 3; codeine muscle 1.6 and femoral blood 0.4, but a paired 0.16; methamphetamine vitreous humour 23.6 and femoral blood 3.8, but a paired 0.89 (4 results in each table).
reporting_issues.consequence: Drug-level ratios should be taken from Table 3 with its numbers of results, not from Table 2 (editors' calculation of the Table 2 contrasts: about 16, 4 and 6 times femoral blood); the across-drug summaries of Table 2 carry the same case-mix problem.

reporting_issues.issue: Sources disagree for the same drug and specimen without comment: amitriptyline vitreous humour 2.1 (mean of 40 cases, Table 4) against 0.15 (median of 20 results, Table 3), and amitriptyline liver 2.5 (Table 4) against 13.77 (Table 3); the text notes only that the Table 4 liver value is surprisingly low.
reporting_issues.consequence: Between-source heterogeneity is large and unexamined; single-drug values rest on whichever sources happened to be found.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists quetiapine with a post-mortem femoral-blood mean of 0.62 mg/L and a median of 0.9 mg/L, a median above the mean, which is unusual for concentration data; the protein-binding column, headed in per cent, prints fractions (for example 0.94).
reporting_issues.consequence: The quetiapine reference median, which sets all its Table 2 ratios, may be a transcription error; the source (Launiainen & Ojanperä 2014) would settle it.

reporting_issues.issue: The reference list uses the number 392 twice (Jantos & Skopp 2013 on methadone; Houts et al. 1998, Courtroom Toxicology), and Table 5 cites 392 for both methadone and paracetamol; the 388 studies of the Abstract cannot be matched to the numbered list, which mixes background and data sources.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the sources behind individual table cells can only be traced approximately.
